questions.knowledge_point: Computing a Differential in a Geometrical Context
questions.problem: Given a rectangular solid, find the differential $\text{d}S$ for the surface area $S$ of the rectangular solid if the base is a square with the side of $a=3$ and the height is $h=7.$
questions.worked_solution:
The surface area of the given rectangular solid is $S=2{a}^{2}+4ah.$ Let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}S(a,h) & =(\frac{∂S}{∂a})\,\text{d}a+(\frac{∂S}{∂h})\,\text{d}h \\  & =(4a+4h)\,\text{d}a+4a\,\text{d}h\end{aligned}
$$

For $a=3$ and $h=7,$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}S(3,7) & =(4\cdot 3+4\cdot 7)\,\text{d}a+4\cdot 3\,\text{d}h \\  & =40\,\text{d}a+12\,\text{d}h.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Using Differentials to Approximate the Value of a Function
questions.problem: Estimate $\operatorname{cos}⁡(1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(0.12)$ using a differential $\text{d}f$ of the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y$ at the point $(\frac{\pi }{3},0).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point $(\frac{\pi }{3},0),$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})\operatorname{sin}⁡0\,\text{d}x+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})\operatorname{cos}⁡0\,\text{d}y \\  & =0\,\text{d}x+\frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we move to the point $(\frac{\pi }{3}+Δx,0+Δy),$ then we can approximate the change in $f$ as

$$
Δf≈0\,Δx+\frac{1}{2}\,Δy
$$

Note that 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(0.12)=f(1,0.12),
$$

so we want to move to the point $(1,0.12).$

Moving from $(\frac{\pi }{3},0)$ to $(1,0.12),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δx & =1-\frac{\pi }{3}, \\ Δy & =0.12-0=0.12.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δf & ≈0\cdot (1-\frac{\pi }{3})+\frac{1}{2}\cdot (0.12) \\  & ≈0+0.5\cdot 0.12 \\  & ≈0.06.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that the value of $f$ increases by about $0.06.$ Consequently, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,0.12) & ≈f(\frac{\pi }{3},0)+0.06 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(0.12) & ≈\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+0.06 \\  & ≈0+0.06 \\  & ≈0.06.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Using Differentials to Approximate the Value of a Function
questions.problem: Estimate $(1.06)^{4.1}$ using a differential $\text{d}f$ of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{y}$ at the point $(1,4).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y \\  & =y{x}^{y-1}\,\text{d}x+{x}^{y}\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point $(1,4),$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =4\cdot {1}^{3}\,\text{d}x+{1}^{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)\,\text{d}y \\  & =4\,\text{d}x+0\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we move to the point $(1+Δx,4+Δy),$ then we can approximate the change in $f$ as

$$
Δf≈4\,Δx+0\,Δy.
$$

Note that 

$$
(1.06)^{4.1}=f(1.06,4.1),
$$

so we want to move to the point $(1.06,4.1).$

Moving from $(1,4)$ to $(1.06,4.1),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δx & =1.06-1=0.06, \\ Δy & =4.1-4=0.1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δf & ≈4\cdot (0.06)+0\cdot (0.1) \\  & ≈0.24+0 \\  & ≈0.24\,.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that the value of $f$ increases by about $0.24.$ Consequently, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1.06,4.1) & ≈f(1,4)+0.24 \\ (1.06)^{4.1} & ≈{1}^{4}+0.24 \\  & ≈1+0.24 \\  & ≈1.24\,.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Using Differentials to Approximate the Change in a Multivariable Function
questions.problem: If $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+4\operatorname{ln}⁡({z}^{3}-y),$ use the differential $\text{d}f$ to estimate the change $Δf$ in the value of $f(x,y,z)$ from $(2,-3,1)$ to $(1,-2,2).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y,z) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y+(\frac{∂f}{∂z})\,\text{d}z \\  & =2x\,\text{d}x-(\frac{4}{{z}^{3}-y})\,\text{d}y+(\frac{12{z}^{2}}{{z}^{3}-y})\,\text{d}z\end{aligned}
$$

At the point $(2,-3,1),$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(2,-3,1) & =(2\cdot 2)\,\text{d}x-(\frac{4}{{1}^{3}-(-3)})\,\text{d}y+(\frac{12\cdot {1}^{2}}{{1}^{3}-(-3)})\,\text{d}z \\  & =4\,\text{d}x-\,\text{d}y+3\,\text{d}z.\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we move to the point $(2+Δx,-3+Δy,1+Δz),$ then we can approximate the change in $f$ as

$$
Δf≈4\,Δx-\,Δy+3\,Δz.
$$

Moving from $(2,-3,1)$ to $(1,-2,2),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δx & =1-2=-1, \\ Δy & =-2-(-3)=1 \\ Δz & =2-1=1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δf & ≈4\,Δx-1\,Δy+3\,Δz \\  & ≈4\cdot (-1)-1\cdot 1+3\cdot 1 \\  & ≈-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the value of $f(x,y,z)$ decreases by approximately $-2.$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing a Differential in a Geometrical Context
questions.problem: Given a rectangular solid, find the differential $\text{d}V$ for the volume $V$ of the rectangular solid if the lengths of the sides are $a=6,$ $b=3,$ and $c=8.$
questions.worked_solution:
The volume of the rectangular solid is $V=abc.$ Let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}V(a,b,c) & =(\frac{∂V}{∂a})\,\text{d}a+(\frac{∂V}{∂b})\,\text{d}b+(\frac{∂V}{∂c})\,\text{d}c \\  & =bc\,\text{d}a+ac\,\text{d}b+ab\,\text{d}c\end{aligned}
$$

For $a=6,$ $b=3,$ and $c=8,$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}V(6,3,8) & =3\cdot 8\,\text{d}a+6\cdot 8\,\text{d}b+6\cdot 3\,\text{d}c \\  & =24\,\text{d}a+48\,\text{d}b+18\,\text{d}c.\end{aligned}
$$
